newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: SACKED NZ MINISTER ATTACKS CREEPING PRIVATISATION.
newsitem.headline: SACKED NZ MINISTER ATTACKS CREEPING PRIVATISATION.

text.p: Sacked New Zealand Associate Health Minister Neil Kirton said on Thursday he had been fighting regular privatisation proposals by the coalition government.

"I continued to resist the creeping privatisation that was being proposed in government circles on an almost daily basis," Kirton, an MP of the junior coalition partner New Zealand First, said in a statement.

"In vital policy areas I was combating the vigorous attempts of Mr (Health Minister Bill) English and various health officials to renege on the Coalition Agreement. Their agenda to privatise remains plain," he said.
Kirton had been involved in a long running dispute with English, a conservative National Party MP, over the level of private involvement in health services.

Deputy Prime Minister and New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who said this morning he had sacked Kirton for giving media interviews, said there has always been privatisation in health going back to the 1930s.

"You have got to look at each area and each example where that might arise and examine whether it should be best delivered by a public service or whether there is no capacity to deliver it from the public service," Peters told journalists.

Asked what the coalition agreement's reference to "limited" private involvement meant, Peters said: "There has to be an acknowledgement of the continuation of private involvement as there has been for decades ... We made it very clear NZ First was for a public service run along business-like lines and that is what we are going to have delivered."
Peters said Kirton would be welcome to stay in the NZ First caucus.
"The New Zealand First caucus has a lot of regard for him. I still do, and those decisions (whether to stay or go) are his to make."
"Certainly I would welcome his remaining in the NZ First caucus," Peters said.
He said he would not support retrospective legislation to force MPs who left their party to resign from parliament.

"But I say it is a matter of honour and I've got a record of personally proving that," Peters said, referring to his decision to resign his seat and seek a by-election when he quit parliament in 1993.
Kirton earlier said he would remain an MP but was considering his options.
